analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from counting climate-change damages in the cost side of rulemaking.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Homeland Security Committee without a vote, after 13 Republicans introduced and cosponsored it in July 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies use a dollar figure — the "social cost of carbon" — to put a price on the damage caused by each ton of carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases when deciding whether a rule is worth its cost. This bill would make it illegal for the Energy Department, EPA, Interior, Transportation, and other agencies to use that figure in any rule, guidance, or analysis, or to justify an action with it. Without a way to count climate damages in dollars, the benefits of pollution limits look smaller on paper, making them harder to adopt and easier to strike down. The bill was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Fossil fuel producers — coal, oil, and natural gas companies — would gain, because rules limiting their emissions could no longer count the climate and health damages those emissions cause when weighing costs against benefits. That makes pollution limits look unjustified and weakens the legal footing for stricter regulation.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Energy Department, EPA, Interior, Transportation, the Council on Environmental Quality, FERC, Treasury, Agriculture, Commerce, and HHS from using the social cost of carbon, methane, nitrous oxide, or any greenhouse gas in cost-benefit analyses, rulemaking, guidance, or justifications for actions [S3].

The bill's findings argue the existing estimates lack peer review, skip required public comment, and improperly count global rather than domestic benefits, and notes 38 pending agency actions relied on the interim figures [S3].
Removal of the climate-cost figure would shrink the measured benefits of rules limiting emissions from fossil fuel production and use, reducing compliance costs for producers of coal, oil, and gas.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear climate and pollution damages that agencies could no longer count when deciding whether to act, and stronger rules limiting emissions would become harder to defend in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to climate and pollution damages

drawbacks.text: Supporters argue the social-cost estimates were developed by an unelected interagency working group without adequate public notice and comment or rigorous peer review, used global rather than domestic benefits, and did not follow the discount-rate guidance in OMB Circular A-4 [S3].

Eliminating the metric would not just fix methodology — it would leave agencies with no standard way to value climate damages at all, so rules that prevent large pollution harms could be rejected because their benefits appear artificially small. A court initially enjoined the interim figures, but the Fifth Circuit stayed that injunction in March 2022, and the figures remained in wide use [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated purpose — a transparent, peer-reviewed, domestically focused cost figure — is a legitimate methodological complaint, and a revised estimate could have addressed it. But the bill does not require a better estimate; it bans agencies from considering the cost of greenhouse gas emissions at all, which removes the main tool for justifying pollution limits and would fall hardest on the public through uncounted climate and health damages.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2022, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Lankford introduced the bill on July 21, 2022, with 12 Republican cosponsors [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day — the only action it ever received [S5].
No markup, hearing, vote, or floor action followed, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, leaving the bill dead [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome favored ordinary people over industry: the bill, which would have removed climate damages from regulatory cost-benefit math, never advanced, and agencies continued using the social-cost figures in pending rules. Fossil fuel producers gained nothing beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people, not fossil fuel producers

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting agencies from considering the social cost of greenhouse gases

against.name: Sen. Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill forward in the seven months before the Congress ended; the bill's only action was referral to his committee

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans (13 of 50 in the Senate); no Democrat or independent supported it, and the Democratic committee chair did not advance it.

industries.note: The bill would bar counting the social cost of carbon in any rule affecting coal production or use, shrinking the measured benefits of limits on coal emissions and making them harder to adopt or defend. The public would bear the uncounted climate and health damages.

The bill's findings single out EPA's methane rule for oil and gas sources as relying on the social cost of methane; banning that figure would weaken one of the main justifications for methane limits on the industry. Producers save compliance costs; the public absorbs the pollution.
